x.A: An Auto Scaling group across multiple AZs scales the application tier and survives an AZ failure, and RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby with automatic failover, so there's no single point of failure and no data loss from a server crash.
x.B: A single AZ with a database on one EC2 instance is a single point of failure, and EC2 auto recovery doesn't restore lost data.
x.C: A read replica replicates asynchronously, so data could be lost, and promoting it is a manual step with downtime.
x.D: EBS Multi-Attach works only within a single AZ, so it can't give shared storage across AZs, and self-managing database clustering is complex.

x.A: By default, Kinesis Data Streams keeps data for only 24 hours. Since the application reads every other day, older records have expired. Extending the retention period fixes the missing data.
x.B: The KPL helps producers batch and send data efficiently, but it doesn't change how long records are kept.
x.C: More shards increase throughput, but records are still deleted after 24 hours.
x.D: S3 Versioning keeps versions of objects but can't recover data that was never written.

x.A: A resource-based policy on a Lambda function controls who can invoke the function. It doesn't give the function permission to call S3.
x.B: Signing requests with a user's credentials inside the function means hard-coding long-term keys, which is insecure.
x.C: Putting an IAM user's credentials in the function still means long-term keys in code, which isn't secure.
x.D: An execution role with the S3 permissions, attached to the Lambda function, gives it temporary credentials automatically. That's the recommended way.

x.A: A 15 minute timeout helps long-running executions, but the problem is that many documents weren't processed during a burst, so it doesn't address lost events.
x.B: Replication copies objects to another bucket and doesn't retry processing.
x.C: Load balancing between two Lambda functions isn't possible this way and doesn't buffer bursts.
x.D: An SQS queue buffers the upload events, and Lambda processes them from the queue with retries. Documents aren't dropped when there's a spike in uploads.

x.A: ALB capacity is managed by AWS and scales automatically, so you don't scale it with Auto Scaling.
x.B: An internet gateway is a managed, highly available component that doesn't need scaling.
x.C: Launching instances in multiple Regions adds complexity and cost and doesn't address scaling by itself.
x.D: A target tracking policy on average CPU adds and removes instances automatically as traffic changes during working hours.
x.E: Scheduled scaling sets the group's capacity to zero on weekends, saving cost when the system isn't needed, and restores it at the start of the week.

x.A: A deny rule on a network ACL for outbound 3306 doesn't allow the DB access and could break needed traffic.
x.B: Allowing the whole public subnet CIDR on 3306 lets anything in that subnet reach the database, which is broader than only the web servers.
x.C: A security group for the web servers that allows inbound 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 opens them to the internet on HTTPS only.
x.D: The DB security group allows port 3306 only from the web servers' security group, so only the web servers can connect.
x.E: Security groups can't contain deny rules, because they allow traffic only.

x.A: DataSync copies data between storage systems and doesn't share data as a mountable Lustre file system.
x.B: A file gateway provides NFS and SMB, not Lustre.
x.C: EFS is NFS-based and can't be configured to support Lustre.
x.D: FSx for Lustre is a fully managed file system that Lustre clients can mount.

x.A: Route 53 failover is DNS-based, so failover is slower because of DNS caching, and an NLB can't invoke a Lambda function directly.
x.B: Global Accelerator supports UDP and routes devices to the nearest healthy Region over the AWS network with fast failover. An NLB handles UDP and forwards to ECS Fargate tasks that process the data.
x.C: An ALB doesn't support UDP, so it can't receive the devices' traffic.
x.D: Route 53 failover is slower, and an ALB doesn't support UDP.

x.A: RDS is a database service and doesn't provide a Windows file share.
x.B: Storage Gateway is a hybrid service that caches data on premises and isn't the most resilient, durable file share for applications running in AWS.
x.C: FSx for Windows File Server provides a fully managed SMB file share that IIS servers can use, and a Multi-AZ deployment makes it highly resilient and durable.
x.D: EFS uses NFS and isn't supported on Windows instances.

x.A: An IAM role can't specify EBS encryption for volumes.
x.B: Creating the volumes as encrypted volumes ensures that data written to them is encrypted at rest.
x.C: A tag doesn't encrypt anything. It's only metadata.
x.D: A KMS key policy controls who can use the key and can't enforce that all EBS volumes are encrypted.

x.A: DynamoDB is a NoSQL database, so moving a MySQL application to it would need database modifications.
x.B: RDS for MySQL needs no modification but you pay for a provisioned instance all the time, which is wasteful for sporadic usage.
x.C: Aurora Serverless is MySQL compatible, so no database changes are needed, and it scales capacity up and down with demand, so the company pays for what it uses with sporadic usage.
x.D: MySQL on EC2 in an Auto Scaling group needs management and doesn't scale a database well.

x.A: GuardDuty detects threats but doesn't monitor bucket policies for remediation like this, and custom remediation code adds work.
x.B: Trusted Advisor only reports, and manual changes are slow and error-prone.
x.C: Resource Access Manager shares resources and doesn't find public buckets.
x.D: S3 Block Public Access at the account level keeps all buckets and objects private, and an SCP stops users from changing the setting, so it's enforced with no custom code.

x.A: A separate EC2 email tier means running and maintaining mail servers, so it's more operational work and doesn't fix delivery issues.
x.B: SES is a managed email service that handles sending at scale and deliverability, so the company no longer has to resolve complex email delivery issues itself.
x.C: SNS can send simple email notifications but isn't designed for marketing and order confirmation email at scale.
x.D: EC2 email servers in an Auto Scaling group still mean managing mail servers and delivery issues.

x.A: A scheduled DataSync task at the end of each day isn't near real time.
x.B: An S3 File Gateway presents a network share that the business system writes to, and the files are stored in S3 almost immediately, with no scheduling or scripts.
x.C: DataSync with API automation means building and maintaining an application, which is more overhead.
x.D: An SFTP endpoint with a polling script means writing and maintaining the script.

x.A: A lifecycle rule moving objects to Intelligent-Tiering automatically optimizes cost for data with unknown or changing access patterns, with no analysis and no retrieval fees.
x.B: Analyzing each object and moving it manually takes a lot of operational effort for petabytes of data.
x.C: Glacier Instant Retrieval has retrieval fees, which could cost a lot for data accessed frequently.
x.D: One Zone-IA has retrieval fees and lower resilience, and not all data is infrequently accessed.

x.A: Redshift is a data warehouse for analytics and doesn't speed up OLTP page loads.
x.B: CloudFront caches static content and speeds up dynamic content for global users, which reduces page load time.
x.C: Dynamic content can't be hosted in S3, since S3 serves only static content.
x.D: A read replica takes read traffic off the primary database, which speeds up database-driven pages.
x.E: Multi-AZ improves availability, not performance, since the standby doesn't serve reads.

x.A: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan covers only EC2 and not Lambda, so the savings on Lambda are missed.
x.B: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan doesn't cover Lambda, and connecting to a public subnet isn't how Lambda reaches private instances.
x.C: A Compute Savings Plan covers EC2 and Lambda and stays valid as usage changes. Connecting the functions to the private subnet that holds the EC2 instances keeps latency low.
x.D: Functions in the Lambda service VPC can't directly reach EC2 instances in the private subnet.

x.A: AdministratorAccess gives far more access than needed, so it violates least privilege.
x.B: Adding the development account as a principal in the role's trust policy lets the development users assume the role in production, which grants only the S3 access that the role allows.
x.C: Turning off Block Public Access would expose the bucket and has nothing to do with cross-account access for the team.
x.D: Creating separate production users for each member adds credentials to manage, and a role is more secure.

x.A: Turning on EBS encryption by default for the Region with a default key makes every new volume encrypted automatically, so employees aren't affected.
x.B: Permission boundaries attach to users and roles, not to organizational units.
x.C: An SCP that denies ec2:CreateVolume when ec2:Encrypted is false, attached at the root OU, stops unencrypted volumes in all accounts, including for root users of member accounts.
x.D: Updating IAM policies in each account is a lot of work and doesn't cover root users.
x.E: Default EBS encryption is set in each account and Region, not once from the management account for all accounts.

x.A: A Multi-AZ DB instance deployment typically fails over in 60 to 120 seconds, not under 40, and a separate read replica adds cost.
x.B: A Multi-AZ DB cluster has two readable standbys already, so creating two additional read replicas adds unnecessary cost.
x.C: The secondary instance in a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment can't serve reads.
x.D: A Multi-AZ DB cluster has two readable standby instances, fails over typically in under 35 seconds, and offers a reader endpoint to offload reads without extra read replicas. It's the lowest-cost fit.

x.A: EBS volumes can't be attached to a Transfer Family endpoint.
x.B: Transfer Family offers a serverless SFTP service. EFS provides high IOPS performance, an internet-facing VPC endpoint with Elastic IPs and a security group restricts trusted IPs, and you control user permissions.
x.C: S3 doesn't give the high IOPS performance, and a public endpoint doesn't give security group control over trusted IPs.
x.D: An internal endpoint in a private subnet isn't internet-facing, so external trusted sources couldn't connect, and S3 doesn't give high IOPS.

x.A: An NLB can't invoke Lambda for asynchronous batches, and Lambda isn't designed to load 1 GB of model data at each startup for requests.
x.B: App Mesh is a service mesh and doesn't scale ECS by queue size, and an ALB isn't an asynchronous request queue.
x.C: Lambda functions can't have vCPUs scaled with Auto Scaling, and loading 1 GB of model data at each start is a poor fit.
x.D: SQS queues the asynchronous requests, and ECS services run the models as containers that load the data once and read from the queue. Auto Scaling on queue size scales from zero to many during irregular batches.

x.A: Identity-based policies can be attached to IAM roles, which is how you give permissions to services and applications.
x.B: Identity-based policies can be attached to IAM groups to give all users in the group the permissions.
x.C: An organization isn't an IAM principal, and service control policies are a different type of policy.
x.D: ECS resources can't have identity-based policies attached. Resource-based policies work differently.
x.E: EC2 resources can't have identity-based policies attached. An instance gets permissions through a role.

x.A: Fargate for the backend costs more than Spot Instances and changes the compute model.

x.C: Spot Instances for always-on frontend nodes risk interruption, and Reserved Instances for backend nodes that run briefly waste money.
x.D: Spot for the frontend risks interruptions, and Fargate costs more for the backend.

x.A: gp2 ties IOPS to volume size, so you can't provision performance independently of capacity.
x.B: io2 allows independent IOPS but costs much more than needed for 15,000 IOPS.
x.C: gp3 lets you provision IOPS (up to 16,000) and throughput independently of the volume size and costs less than gp2 or io volumes. 15,000 IOPS fits within its limit.
x.D: io1 also provides independent IOPS but at a higher price than gp3.
